title: Big-O Notation
description: Learn the universal language of algorithm performance. This lesson introduces **Big-O Notation**, the mathematical framework used by software engineers to describe how an algorithm's runtime or memory requirements grow as the amount of input data increases.

sections.title: Introduction to Big-O
sections.content: When comparing two algorithms, it is not enough to measure execution time in seconds. A faster computer will run a bad algorithm faster than a slow computer running a good algorithm. Instead, we need a way to measure efficiency based purely on the **number of operations** relative to the **input size (n)**.

subsections.title: What is Big-O?
subsections.content: **Big-O Notation** is the universal language used by computer scientists to describe performance. It expresses the **upper bound** of an algorithm's growth rate. Simply put, it tells us: *As the amount of data gets infinitely large, how quickly does the required time (or memory) shoot up?*

sections.title: The Worst-Case Scenario
sections.content: When measuring efficiency, programmers generally care most about the **worst-case scenario**. If you are searching for a specific name in a phone book, you might get lucky and find it on the very first page. However, we cannot base our performance metrics on luck.

subsections.title: Preparing for the Worst
subsections.content: Big-O assumes the data is arranged in the worst possible way for your algorithm. If you are searching an array of `n` items, Big-O assumes the item you are looking for is at the **very end of the array** (or not there at all), forcing your algorithm to do the maximum amount of work. This guarantees that your algorithm will **never perform worse** than its Big-O rating.

sections.title: The Rules of Big-O
sections.content: When calculating the Big-O of an algorithm, we don't care about exact numbers. We only care about the **overall trend** as `n` approaches infinity. Because of this, we follow two strict mathematical rules.

subsections.title: Rule 1: Drop the Constants
subsections.content: If an algorithm requires `2n` operations, we drop the `2` and simply call it **O(n)**. If it requires `n / 2` operations, it is still **O(n)**. As data grows to a billion items, the constant multiplier becomes insignificant compared to the sheer size of `n`.

subsections.title: Rule 2: Drop Non-Dominant Terms
subsections.content: If an algorithm does an `O(n²)` operation followed by an `O(n)` operation, the total time is `O(n² + n)`. However, as `n` gets huge, the `n²` part completely overshadows the `n` part. Therefore, we only keep the **largest, fastest-growing term**.

sections.title: Calculating Big-O in Code
sections.content: To calculate the Big-O of your AlgoBlocks code, look directly at how you are using your control structures (specifically, loops).

subsections.title: Code Examples
subsections.content: Here is how common programming structures translate into Big-O notation:
bullets: **O(1):** Basic math, setting a variable, or accessing an array index. There are no loops involved.
**O(n):** A single loop that iterates over a list of `n` items.
**O(n²):** A loop perfectly **nested** inside another loop. (For every item in `n`, we loop through `n` again).

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: Big-O Notation is how software engineers communicate efficiency. By dropping constants and non-dominant terms, it allows us to focus entirely on **scalability**.

subsections.title: Key Takeaways
subsections.content: Remember these core principles as you analyze algorithms:
bullets: Look for **nested loops** to quickly estimate complexity.
